questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Giving a lethal injection to end a patient's suffering is:
questions.rationale: Active euthanasia kills by active means, e.g., a lethal drug dose; passive euthanasia withholds life support.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Types of euthanasia (PDF p. 97)
questions.quote: Active euthanasia: killing a patient by active means

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A doctor gives a patient pills so the patient can end his own life. This is:
questions.rationale: In physician-assisted suicide, the physician provides the means and the patient administers it.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Types of euthanasia (PDF p. 97)
questions.quote: A physician provides the patient with a means, such as sufficient medication, for the patient to kill him or herself.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A dying patient is kept on machines with no regard for quality of life, only extending dying. This is:
questions.rationale: Dysthanasia extends the dying process through technology without regard to quality of life.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Dysthanasia (PDF p. 98)
questions.quote: has their biological life extended through technological means without regard to the person's quality of life

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A poor patient dies early in pain because treatable care was not available. This is called:
questions.rationale: Misthanasia (miserable death) includes deaths from lack of care, malpractice or abandonment.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Misthanasia (PDF p. 98)
questions.quote: Social euthanasia, or misthanasia (miserable death)

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Which approach helps a terminal patient die well, avoiding both hastening and prolonging death?
questions.rationale: Orthothanasia, the art of dying well, rejects euthanasia and dysthanasia and focuses on caring.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Orthothanasia (PDF p. 98)
questions.quote: Orthothanagia (art Of dying well) rejects all forms Of misthanasia without, however, falling into the trap of euthanasia or dysthanasia.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A terminally ill patient stops a painful treatment because the suffering is intolerable. Ethically, this is:
questions.rationale: Refusing intolerable treatment intends the end of suffering, not death, so it is not regarded as suicide.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Ethics of the patient (PDF p. 98)
questions.quote: we view refusing treatment not a suicide by common sense or practical wisdom standards

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Treatment of a terminal patient's disease is stopped with consent. What must continue?
questions.rationale: It may be ethical to omit treatment, but never to omit care; dignity must be respected.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Cooperation with refusal (PDF p. 100)
questions.quote: But it is not ethical to omit care, since human dignity is to be respected.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Staff do a deliberately slow, half-hearted resuscitation to satisfy a family. This 'slow code' is:
questions.rationale: The slow code deceives families and avoids public responsibility; decisions belong in a written order.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 The no-code order (PDF p. 102)
questions.quote: the deception involved should be condemned

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A do-not-resuscitate order is valid when it is:
options: Written and justified in the chart
questions.rationale: A no-code order is a written order for which the physician accepts responsibility, justified on the chart.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 The no-code order (PDF p. 102)
questions.quote: this is a %Titten order for which the physician accepts public responsibility and that should be medially justified on the chart

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: An order says 'chest compressions yes, intubation no.' This is a:
questions.rationale: A partial code is a written order to omit some interventions and use others, with reasons charted.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Partial code (PDF p. 102)
questions.quote: The partial ode is a written order to omit some medical interventions, but to employ others.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A dying patient's visiting hours are limited. What does humanly intensive care call for?
questions.rationale: As death nears, limits on visits should be removed; even prepared children may visit to say goodbye.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Care for the dying (PDF p. 103)
questions.quote: Limits on visits should be removed.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A terminal cancer patient says his pain is 8/10 but is lying still. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: The patient's own report is what matters; waiting for 'objective' signs leaves pain untreated.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Pain control (PDF p. 103)
questions.quote: when the patient says he is in pain, his judgnent should be the one that matters

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A family fears their dying father will become addicted to morphine. The nurse explains that:
questions.rationale: Narcotics used properly for pain are not addictive; dependence reflects persistent pain.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Pain control (PDF p. 103)
questions.quote: even powerful narcotics like morphine are not addictive when used properly to treat pain

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Morphine is given to relieve a dying patient's pain, though it may depress breathing. This is justified by:
questions.rationale: Under double effect, the intended effect is pain relief; possible respiratory depression is foreseen, not intended.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Hastening death (PDF p. 106)
questions.quote: the nurse or clinician should always consider what the intended effect of the intervention is

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: How does palliative sedation differ from euthanasia?
options: Its intent is relief, not death
It is done early in illness
questions.rationale: Palliative sedation aims to relieve refractory suffering; euthanasia intends to cause death.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Palliative sedation (PDF p. 107)
questions.quote: The intent is not to hasten denth but to relieve suffering that cannot be relieved by any other available method.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Which is a criterion for palliative sedation?
options: Death is expected in hours to days
questions.rationale: Criteria: terminal illness, intolerable refractory symptoms, DNR in effect, and death imminent (hours to days).
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Criteria for palliative sedation (PDF p. 107)
questions.quote: Death is imminent (hours to days)

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A patient asks the nurse to help him end his life with an overdose. The nurse should:
options: Tell him to ask a relative
questions.rationale: Nursing ethics codes prohibit involvement in assisted dying; the nurse explores and relieves suffering.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Assisted dying (PDF p. 107)
questions.quote: The vast rnnjority of ethical codes from the main nurses' organizations prohibit the involvement or a nurse in the assisted dying of patients.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: What is the role of a hospital ethics committee?
questions.rationale: Ethics committees educate, develop policies and act as advisory consultants; their advice is not legally binding.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Ethics committees (PDF p. 108)
questions.quote: Third, they are to act as advisory consultants to health care providers and possibly families

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Is a physician legally required to follow an ethics committee's recommendation?
questions.rationale: There is no legal duty to follow ethics committee recommendations; they do not replace judicial review.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Ethics committees (PDF p. 109)
questions.quote: There is no legal duty to follow the recommendations of an ethics committee.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: As a patient nears death, the family should be treated as:
questions.rationale: Family members become secondary patients who need information and emotional support.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 The family in death and dying (PDF p. 109)
questions.quote: At a certain point in the dying process, the family members become secondary patients

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A competent, non-terminal patient refuses a medically indicated treatment. Who may overrule him?
questions.rationale: The competent patient keeps the right to refuse; only a court order or court-appointed guardian can overrule.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Refusal by a nonterminal patient (PDF p. 101)
questions.quote: Only a court order or a court-appointed guardian has the right to overrule the patient in these cases.
